## The one-liner

> We integrated application, case management, and federal reporting data so that
> Church at the Park can has better understanding of what factors affect entry into, and exit from, emergency shelter.

**Role:** I lead data wrangling for applications and survival analysis, and was team lead.

**Team:** Jon Garrow, Mike Kimmell, Summer Tucker

**Repo:** [https://github.com/stuckerWU/data510-capstone](https://github.com/stuckerWU/data510-capstone)

## The question

Church at the Park’s (C@P) program data, including shelter and
housing applications, demographics, assessments, and case notes
live in 3 disconnected systems. In this project, we explored how the
data can be joined together to provide insights on program
delivery, average times post-application and in stays, and what is
predictive of positive exits.
Through this work we hope to help Church at the Park’s staff better
understand their program outcomes and advocate for increased
resources that will lead to more community benefit. 

Our project investigates the following questions:

● Can we construct a sustainable data engineering pipeline that
integrates C@P’s 3 program datasets?

● What insights can we derive from integrated data to improve
service delivery and support decision-making? Specifically:

  - Are there factors that are correlated to the average length of
wait to get into shelter, and the average stay in shelter?

  - Are there factors that are correlated to whether a participant
is successful getting into shelter, more likely to return to C@P
for services, or contribute to successful exit from emergency
shelter?

## The data

Our data came directly from C@P, provided to us with their permission. We integrated three data sources to conduct our analysis:

● C@P’s application platform

● Case notes from C@P's case management platform

● Outcome information for shelter stays 

These sources were combined to create two datasets for analysis: an emergency shelter stay dataset (1,108 rows) and an
application data set (5,393 rows).

## The approach

We took two approaches to analyzing CAP's research question:

(1) Survival analysis: A statistical approach to evaluate how long
participants take to enter and exit shelter, and explore which
variables modify the time it takes to enter or exit. 
This analysis provided us insights into what factors affect how long a participant waits to get into shelter, or stays in shelter. 

(2) Machine learning: We used XGBoost, amachine learning algorithm, to examine qualities that
lead to successful entry to shelter, or successful successful exit
from shelter. 
This analysis provided us insights on predicting successful entry into shelter, or exiting to a positive housing outcome. Our model for 
entry into shelter was not very predictive, but we found some success in predicting exit to a positive housing outcome.


## Findings

We found multiple factors affect the timeframes to get into, or exit, shelter. 

*Specific circumstances or traits of the participant*

We found notable differences in time spent in or waiting for
shelter depending on:

● Shelter location

● Whether the participant has
health coverage

● Gender

● Age

*Level of engagement in case management.*

Our data sources include case management notes that summarize assistance
participants were receiving from a case manager. We found multiple variables where more
engagement appears associated with longer stays in shelter.

Those factors include:

● The count of appointments,
and the count of the number
of times appointment was
mentioned in a case note.

● Higher mentions of the words
“medication”, “identification”
and “benefits” were also
associated with longer stays.
